title: How the Bicycle Freed Women — And Why The Church Tried to Ban It | Weird History
fullText: In 1896, a 76-year-old woman sat down with one of the most famous journalists in America, a reporter named Nelly Bllye and said something that sounded completely ridiculous. Susan B. Anthony, the woman who had spent her entire adult life fighting for the right to vote, told Bllye that a bicycle had done more to free women than anything else in the world. Not the printing press, not the telegraph, not education reform, a bicycle. And the wild part is she was probably right because this two- wheeled contraption managed to do something that decades of pamphlets, petitions, and protest marches couldn't pull off. It killed the corset. It destroyed chaperone dating. It emptied church pews on Sunday mornings. It terrified doctors into inventing a fake disease. And it made conservative clergymen so furious that one Atlanta pastor stood up in front of his congregation and declared that the bicycle woman had been entered by Satan himself. All of that from a machine you can buy at Walmart for 150 bucks. So how did a piece of metal and rubber become the most dangerous object in the Victorian world? London England 1,880. If you were a middle-class woman living in a city like London or New York or Boston at the end of the 19th century, your world was shockingly small. And that smallalness was by design. Victorian society ran on something called the doctrine of separate spheres. Men belonged to the public world, the offices and factories and streets. Women belonged to the private world, the parlor and the kitchen and the nursery. A respectable woman did not simply walk out her front door and go wherever she pleased. She needed a reason, a destination, and above all, she needed a chaperone. Think about what that actually meant for a second. You could not leave your own house alone. If you wanted to visit a friend across town, you needed a male escort or an older female companion. If you wanted to go shopping, someone had to come with you. If you wanted to see the man you were courting, you had to do it in the parlor of your parents' home with your mother watching from the next room. Your physical geography was controlled by the people around you, and transportation made it worse. Horses and carriages were expensive. In a city, stabling a horse could cost more than renting an apartment. So unless your family had serious money, you were walking. And walking in the clothes that Victorian women were expected to wear was its own special kind of punishment. The average woman in the 1880s wore roughly 37 lbs of clothing. That is not an exaggeration. There were layers of petticoats, a whale bone corset cinched so tight it displaced internal organs, a bustle strapped to the lower back, and a skirt that swept the floor and collected mud and horse manure with every step. Women fainted regularly, not because they were delicate, but because their corsets compressed their lungs to the point where they could not breathe properly. Doctors of the era recorded cases of broken ribs, displaced livers, and crushed stomachs, all from corsets. And this was considered normal. This was just what being a woman looked like. Now into this world, drop the bicycle, not the modern bicycle. The early ones were terrible. The Velociped of the 1860s was a bone rattling iron contraption that earned the nickname bone shaker for obvious reasons. Then came the penny farthing in the 1870s with its enormous front wheel and tiny rear wheel. Riding a penny farthing required athletic skill, serious nerve, and a willingness to break your neck because the rider sat 5 ft off the ground directly behind the front axle, hit a rock, and you'd go flying over the handlebars head first. Head over handlebars accidents were so common that they literally invented the phrase taking a header to describe the experience. The penny farthing was a rich man's daredevil sport. Women were completely excluded. There was no way to ride one in a floorlength skirt and the danger was considered wildly inappropriate for the so-called weaker sex. So for decades the bicycle existed in its various forms and women watched from the sidewalk. Meanwhile, feminists were fighting a completely different battle over clothes. In 1851, a woman named Amelia Bloomer published an article in her newspaper, The Lily, calling for dress reform. She and her supporters started wearing half-length skirts over loose Turkish trousers. What the press immediately started calling bloomers. The reaction was savage. Newspapers mocked them. Cartoonists drew them as mananish freaks. Men harassed them in the street. The backlash was so vicious that Bloomer herself abandoned the outfit by 1859, saying the newly invented kinolin was reform enough. 40 years of feminist fashion advocacy and the corset was still going strong. The bloomer was dead. Women were still trapped in their parlors wearing 37 lb of fabric. Unable to walk more than a few blocks without exhausting themselves. Then in 1885, a British engineer named John Kemp Stley did something that would accidentally reshape Western civilization. He built a bicycle with two wheels the same size. Starly called it the Rover. It had two wheels the same size, a chain drive system connecting the pedals to the rear wheel, and a frame low enough that the rider could put both feet flat on the ground while sitting on the seat. No more sitting 5t in the air on a giant wheel praying you didn't hit a pothole. No more acrobatic mounts and dismounts. Just sit down, push the pedals, and go. 3 years later, in 1888, a Scottish veterinarian named John Boyd Dunlop was watching his son bounce along a cobblestone street on a tricycle with solid rubber tires. The kid was miserable, so Dunlop glued a rubber hose into a loop, inflated it with a football pump, and wrapped it around the wheel. That crude experiment became the pneumatic tire, and it transformed the bicycle from a bumpy, jarring ordeal into something that actually felt good to ride. These two inventions together, equal-sized wheels and airfilled tires, created what the Victorians called the safety bicycle. And the name was the whole point. This was a bicycle that ordinary people could ride. People who were not athletes, people who were not daredevils, people who were, for example, women wearing long skirts. The numbers tell you how fast this caught on. In 1889, manufacturers worldwide produced roughly 200,000 bicycles. By 1896, American factories alone were building over 400,000 a year. By 1899, global production had crossed 1 million units. In 1897, Americans bought more than 2 million bicycles, which works out to about one for every 30 people in the country. 5,000 workers in downtown Chicago rode their bicycles to work every single day. The bicycle was not a fad. It was a transportation revolution happening in real time. And the price made it democratic. A horse and carriage could cost a working family's entire annual income. A bicycle cost a fraction of that, and manufacturers offered payment plans. For the first time in history, a woman could own her own vehicle. Not her husband's vehicle, not her father's vehicle, hers. But here's the detail that everyone missed at the time. The bicycle did not just give women a way to get around. It gave them a way to get around alone. There was no passenger seat on a safety bicycle. There was no room for a chaperone. When a woman climbed onto that saddle and started pedaling, she was by definition unsupervised. And in the Victorian world, an unsupervised woman was the most terrifying thing imaginable. Suddenly, a young woman in Boston or London or Paris could ride 6 miles to meet a friend without asking anyone's permission. She could pedal across town to a lecture or a political meeting without a male escort watching her every move. She could meet a young man in a park three neighborhoods away, and her parents would have absolutely no idea. The bicycle collapsed, what you might call dating geography. Before the bike, courtship happened in your parlor under the watchful eye of your mother. After the bike, courtship happened wherever you could pedal to in an afternoon. Bikes facilitated unshaperon dates. They facilitated elopments. An editorial in 1896 put it perfectly when it described the bicycle as a steed on which women rode into a new world. God's magazine, one of the most popular women's publications of the era, declared that with the bicycle in her possession. The daughter of the 19th century could feel that her declaration of independence had been proclaimed. And this was not just happening in America. By 1890, the cyclists touring club in Britain had 60,000 members and a full third of them, 20,000, were women. Women formed exclusive cycling clubs with their own newsletters, uniforms, and competitions. They organized group rides that doubled as political organizing sessions. The popular press started calling these women revoling daughters, a term the women wore as a badge of honor before it eventually softened into the more [music] respectable label of the new woman. The new woman rode a bicycle. She wore practical clothing. She went where she wanted when she wanted with whoever she wanted and she did not ask permission. Beatrice Grimshaw, an adventurer and writer from Ireland, captured what the bicycle meant to this generation when she recalled her girlhood. She said she bought a bicycle and rode unshaperoned, miles and miles beyond the limits possible to the soberly trottting horses. The world opened before her. She went away from home to see what the world might give to daughters who revolted. And the timing of what happened next was almost too perfect. Because the moment women started riding in significant numbers, the establishment panicked. Doctors, clergymen, newspaper editors, and politicians all converged on the same conclusion. The bicycle had to be stopped. The doctors came first and they came swinging. A British physician named A. Shadwell published warnings that cycling would cause permanent disfigurement in women. He called it bicycle face, a condition where a woman's features would become fixed in a strained, exhausted, wildeyed grimace from the physical effort of pedaling. Her jaw would clench, her eyes would bulge, dark circles would form, and according to Shadwell, this was not temporary. Bicycle face was permanent. Once you had it, your beauty was gone forever. The Literary Digest picked up the story in September of 1895 and ran with it, warning that overexertion on the wheel, combined with the effort of maintaining balance, would produce this disfigurement in any woman foolish enough to ride. Medical journals across England and America started debating bicycle face as if it were a real clinical diagnosis. Doctors wrote papers about it. Newspapers quoted those papers and women were told in all seriousness that riding a bicycle would make them ugly for life. And that was only the beginning of the medical case against women on bicycles. Shadwell also reported observing a healthy girl, someone he described as rather stronger than average, collapsed completely after riding just 10 mi further than her usual distance. He went on to list the other conditions he attributed to female cycling. Exofalmic guat, internal inflammation, chronic daentry, appendicitis, headaches, insomnia, depression, complete nervous frustration. Other doctors piled on with their own additions. Tuberculosis, infertility, gout, bow-leggedness, heart disease. The list kept growing because the list was never really about medicine. It was about control. If you could convince women that cycling would destroy their health and ruin their appearance, you could keep them off the bicycle without ever having to admit what you were actually afraid of. In 1897, a Chicago physician named Doctor Sarah Hackett Stevenson had finally had enough. She published a response in the frenological journal stating flatly that cycling was not injurious to any part of the anatomy and that it improved general health. The anxious facial expression everyone kept panicking about, she said, was seen only among beginners and was caused by the uncertainty of amateurs. Bicycle face was not a disease. It was just a new rider learning to balance, which looking back was either incredibly obvious or incredibly brave to say out loud. But if the doctors were bad, the clergymen were worse. Protestant ministers across the United States and Britain saw the bicycle as a direct threat to their authority and they were not subtle about saying so. The first problem was Sunday. For most working people in the 1890s, Sunday was the only day off. And once the bicycle arrived, people started spending that day riding through the countryside instead of sitting in a church pew. Male church attendance had already been declining. Cycling threatened to drain the remaining congregation down to the elderly and the sick. One minister in Indianapolis tried to solve the problem by starting a cycling group for young church members. His own church leadership centured him for it. The second problem was the clothing. Women who rode bicycles needed practical clothing which meant bloomers, shortened skirts or outright trousers. Clergymen of every denomination denounced these outfits from the pulpit. Dr. JB Hawthorne, the pastor of the First Baptist Church of Atlanta, gave a sermon declaring that the new woman movement was born of infidelity. He said the bicycle woman had been entered by Satan and that by coveting the prerogatives, honors, and pleasures of men, she had made herself despicable in the eyes of all people of virtuous sensibilities. And no, that is not a paraphrase. That is genuinely what a Baptist pastor said about women riding bicycles in the 1890s. At a prayer meeting in Bingmpington, New York in 1893, a man named Samuel Stanley stood up and denounced cycling as unladylike, uncchristian, and a disgrace to the church. The pastor, Reverend John Bradshaw, sided with him publicly. In 1895, the board of trustees at the College Point Seminary in Flushing, New York, banned women teachers from riding their bicycles to and from school. The women in question were wearing full skirts, not bloomers, but the board feared that allowing bicycles at all would lead to women wanting to dress like the new women in Manhattan. Better to kill the habit before it started. Then there was the Women's Rescue League of Boston, which managed to combine moral panic with slander. In one spectacular claim, they announced publicly that following the closing of brothel in the city, prostitutes had taken to riding bicycles to reach their clients. The bicycle, in other words, was not just immoral. It was literally a vehicle for prostitution. Across the Atlantic and into the Middle East, the backlash was even more direct. In the Ottoman Empire, conservative religious scholars called the bicycle the devil's chariot. Orthodox authorities claimed that cycling would harm women's reproductive organs, embolden sexual permissiveness, and lead to the destruction of the family. According to Alon Rob, a professor of religious studies at UC Davis, many Muslim religious authorities classified women's cycling as a heretical innovation. In some places, women who rode bicycles faced physical assaults in the street. So, doctors invented a fake disease to scare women off the bicycle. Preachers called it satanic. Morality leagues blamed it for prostitution. And religious scholars in the Ottoman Empire called it heresy. And every single one of them failed. Because while the establishment was busy writing sermons and medical warnings, women were busy doing something far more subversive than riding bicycles. They were changing their clothes. The corset had survived everything. It survived Amelia Bloomer's newspaper editorials in 1851. It survived the Rational Dress Society. Founded in London in 1881 by Vic Countess Florence Harbetton, which spent years politely arguing that women's clothing should not cause organ damage. It survived decades of feminist pamphlets, medical warnings about displaced ribs, and common sense. The corset did not care about your arguments. The corset was fashion, and fashion was more powerful than logic. But the corset could not survive the bicycle. Because you cannot ride a bicycle in a corset, you physically cannot do it. Try to pedal while your torso is locked inside a cage of whale bone and steel. Try to breathe while climbing a hill with your lungs compressed to half capacity. try to balance on two wheels while wearing a skirt so wide it catches in the chain and drags along the rear wheel. The bicycle did not make an ideological argument against the corset. It made a mechanical one. If you wanted to ride, you had to change what you were wearing. Period. And women wanted to ride. So the rational dress movement, which had been treated as a fringe cause for 40 years, suddenly had the most persuasive argument in the world. Not politics, not feminism, practicality. You could not use this machine, this glorious machine that gave you freedom and speed and independence unless you put on different clothes. The bicycle turned dress reform from an abstract debate into an everyday decision. Women started showing up to cycling clubs in bloomers, those loose Turkish style trousers that Amelia Bloomer had been ridiculed for promoting back in the 1850s. Others wore shortened skirts that stopped at the calf instead of dragging on the ground. The more daring women wore outright nicker boxers, tailored tweed suits with kneelength breaches that looked almost identical to what men wore. Corset manufacturers, sensing the shift, scrambled to produce sport corsets with elastic panels and wire instead of bone, lighter and more flexible versions designed for cycling. Even that was a concession. The corset industry was negotiating the terms of its own surrender. And women did not just adapt existing clothing. They invented new clothing. Throughout the 1890s, women filed patents for cycling specific garments. Convertible skirts that could be buttoned up into a trouser-like configuration for riding and let down again for walking. Hidden bifocated skirts that looked like regular dresses from the outside, but divided into two legs underneath. These were engineering solutions to a social problem and they were designed, patented and manufactured by women. A teenage cyclist named Tessy Reynolds demonstrated how serious the movement was getting. In 1893, she completed the Brighton to London and back ride in 8 hours and 38 minutes wearing full rational dress. The cycling press hailed her as a pioneer. The conservative press called her scandalous. The public stared. And none of it mattered because she had just proven that rational clothing made women faster, safer, and more capable on a bicycle. The backlash to the new cycling outfits was real, and sometimes violent. Lady cyclists in bloomers reported being insulted, spat on, and pelted with stones by men on the street. A cartoon published in the Lady Cyclist magazine in 1896 depicted impudent men jeering at a dignified female cyclist, capturing a scene that was playing out on roads across England and America everyday. But the harassment did not stop the movement. It accelerated it. Every woman who rode through the jeering in her bloomers made it slightly easier for the next woman to do the same. The great irony of the whole thing is that Amelia Bloomer had tried to free women from the corset through ideology and persuasion. She failed. The bicycle freed women from the corset through physics. You cannot argue with a chain drive. You cannot debate a pneumatic tire. The machine did not care about your opinions on femininity. It just required you to dress in a way that let you use it. And once women dress that way, they discovered that they liked breathing. They liked moving freely. They liked not fainting. The corset never fully recovered. Now, everything we have talked about so far happened to thousands of anonymous women across two continents. But in June of 1894, one very specific woman decided to take the whole experiment to its absolute extreme. Her name was Annie Cohen Copchovski, and she was about to attempt something that no woman had ever done before. Annie Cohen Copchovski was a 23-year-old Latvian Jewish immigrant living in a tenement in the West End of Boston. She was married to a clothing peddler named Max. She had three children, ages 5, three, and two. She sold advertising space for local newspapers and she had learned to ride a bicycle approximately 3 days before she attempted to ride one around the entire world. That is not a typo, by the way. 3 days. The story, as it was reported at the time, went like this. Two wealthy Boston businessmen made a wager. One bet $20,000 that no woman could circumn the globe on a bicycle. The other took the opposite side. The terms required the woman to complete the journey within 15 months, start out penniless, and earn $5,000 above her expenses along the way. The prize for finishing was $10,000. Whether this bet was real or something Annie invented for publicity purposes has never been fully settled. What is settled is that on the 25th of June 1894 at 11:00 in the morning, Annie Copchovsky climbed onto a 42lb Colombia women's bicycle on the steps of the Massachusetts State House on Beacon Hill and pedled away from everything she knew. She was 5'3. She weighed about 100 lb. She was a Jewish woman traveling alone through a country where anti-semitism was widespread and she had three toddlers at home. Her first smart decision happened before she even left Boston. A representative from the London Derry Lithia Spring Water Company of New Hampshire offered her $100 to carry a placard advertising their product on her bicycle and to go by the name Annie Londereerry for the duration of the trip. She took the money, took the name and buried her Jewish identity under a corporate sponsorship. Annie Copchovsky became Annie Londereerry and Annie Londereerry became famous. The first leg of the trip was a disaster. She rode west from Boston toward Chicago on unpaved roads wearing a long skirt on a bicycle that weighed nearly as much as she did. The Colombia women's model did not have a freewheel mechanism, which meant the pedals never stopped spinning. When she picked up speed going downhill, she had to lift her legs off the pedals entirely and rest her feet on coaster brackets mounted to the front forks to keep her skirts from tangling in the machinery. It took her 3 months just to reach Chicago and she nearly quit. But Annie Copchovsky was not a quitter. She was a self-promoter of extraordinary talent. In Chicago, she traded her 42 lb Colombia for a 21-lb Sterling men's bicycle. half the weight. She ditched the skirt and stitched her bloomers into tighter fitting pants that looked more like a man's riding suit. She strapped a pearl-handled revolver to her hip and she turned around and headed east back toward the Atlantic because she had realized that sailing across the ocean and cycling through foreign countries in short bursts was faster than grinding across the American frontier. From New York, she sailed to France where she became a sensation. She picked up sponsorship after sponsorship. She told the European press she had graduated from Harvard, attended medical school and was an ays. None of it was true. She spoke only English and Yiddish, but claimed to speak German and Swedish. She never mentioned her husband or children, letting audiences assume she was single. Annie Londereerry was inventing herself in real time, and the bicycle was her stage. She sailed from Marseilles through the Suez Canal, stopping in Alexandria, Columbbo, Singapore, Saigon, Hong Kong, and Shanghai. She claimed to have been briefly imprisoned during the SinoJapanese War. In March of 1895, she sailed from Yokohama to San Francisco. Then she got back on the bicycle and rode through southern California, across Arizona, through New Mexico to El Paso, up through Colorado, and across Nebraska. Near Gladbrook, Iowa, she crashed into a drove of pigs, broke her wrist, and wore a cast for the rest of the journey. On the 12th of September, 1895, Annie Londereerry rolled into Chicago, accompanied by two cyclists she had met on the road in Iowa. She had been gone 15 months. She had ridden thousands of miles by bicycle and traveled thousands more by steamship and train. Whether she had technically cycled around the world was debatable. What was not debatable was that a 5'3 Jewish mother of three who had learned to ride a bicycle 72 hours before departure had just circled the planet alone with a pearl revolver and a corporate sponsorship and come home in one piece. She collected her $10,000. She moved her family to New York. She became a journalist for the New York world. And she never rode a bicycle again. Annie London Derry was the most dramatic example of what the bicycle made possible. But the real revolution was not one woman circling the globe. It was millions of women circling their own neighborhoods for the first time without permission. In 1895, the same year, Annie was pedalling through the Arizona desert, one of the most famous women in America, sat down and wrote a book about learning to ride a bicycle. Her name was Francis Willard. She was the founder of the Women's Christian Temperance Union, one of the largest women's organizations in the country, and she was 53 years old. The book was called A Wheel Within a Wheel: How I Learned to Ride the Bicycle, and it was not really about cycling. Willard wrote that she wanted to help women to a wider world. She said she was driven by a natural love of adventure, a love long hampered and impeded, and by a desire to acquire this new implement of power and literally put it underfoot. She was describing a bicycle, but she was talking about freedom. Willard's book became a bestseller, and it captured something that was already happening in cycling clubs across the English-speaking world. Women were not just riding together, they were organizing together. Cycling clubs had newsletters. They had elected officers. They had meetings where women who had never participated in public life before learned how to run an organization, manage a budget, debate strategy, and mobilize a group. The skills women developed in cycling clubs transferred directly into the suffrage movement. The bicycle did not just give women mobility. It gave them infrastructure. But the bicycle's influence stretched beyond women's rights into corners of history that seem completely unrelated. In Dayton, Ohio, two brothers named Wilbur and Orville Wright were running a bicycle shop during the 1890s boom. The Wright Cycle Company designed, manufactured, and sold bicycles. And the profits from that shop funded their real obsession, which was building a machine that could fly. The mechanical knowledge they gained from building lightweight bicycle frames, from working with chains and sprockets and thin metal tubing, fed directly into the design of the 1,93 right flyer at Kittyhawk. The bicycle did not just change how people moved on the ground. It helped put people in the air. And for all the panic it caused in the 1890s, the bicycle was never successfully stopped. Not by doctors, not by preachers, not by morality leagues. Every attempt to ban it or shame women off of it failed completely. The corset industry adapted or collapsed. Church attendance continued to decline for reasons that had nothing to do with wheels. Bicycle face disappeared from medical literature because it had never existed in the first place and women kept riding. But here is the part of this story that should genuinely unsettle you. The fight over women and bicycles is not over. In September of 2016, Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Kami issued a fatwa banning women from cycling in public. His exact reasoning was that riding a bicycle attracts the attention of men and exposes society to corruption and thus contravenes women's chastity. That was 2016, 120 years after Susan B. Anthony celebrated the bicycle as a tool of emancipation. A head of state was still trying to take it away from women for the same reasons the Atlanta preacher had raged about in the 1890s. Iranian women responded exactly the way the new women of the 1890s would have. They kept riding. They posted photographs and videos of themselves on bicycles across social media using the hashtag Iranian women love cycling. The activist Masi Alinagad's my stealthy freedom campaign amplified their defiance to a global audience. Women in Isfahan, a city famous for its cycling lanes and bike sharing system, were detained by police and forced to sign pledges never to cycle again. They signed the pledges. Then they got back on their bicycles. Today, there are more than 1 billion bicycles on the planet. That is more than any other vehicle in existence. The single most produced vehicle model in human history is not a Toyota or a Ford. It is the Chinese flying pigeon bicycle with over 500 million units manufactured. Every year the world produces roughly 130 million new bicycles which is about 2 and a half times the number of cars built in the same period. The bicycle is not a relic. It is the most successful transportation technology ever invented. Susan B. Anthony was 76 years old and nearly blind when she sat across from Nelly Bllye in that 1896 interview. She had spent more than 50 years fighting for women's suffrage. She had been arrested for voting. She had been mocked, threatened, and dismissed by every level of government. She would die 10 years later without ever casting a legal ballot. And yet, when Blie asked her about progress, about what had actually moved the needle for women, Anthony did not talk about speeches or legislation or protests. She talked about a bicycle. She said it gave women a feeling of freedom and self-reliance the moment they took their seat and away they went. The picture of free, untrabled womanhood. She was right. And 130 years later, women are still pedaling.
